justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect. It says that when the native timer returns null or undefined, the else branch evaluates `handleOrId.refresh` and "throws a TypeError inside scheduleTask". It also notes that the old code guarded against a nullish handle. That is the known bug's faulty code and failure mechanism. Finding 1 is about a numeric handle of 0 being treated as falsy by the truthiness checks, which is a different issue.
ground_truth: In `patchTimer`'s `scheduleTask`, the change stores the native timer's return value in `handleOrId`. When it is not a number, it executes `data.isRefreshable = isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)`. Some environments return null or undefined from `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/`requestAnimationFrame`, for example a browser extension, policy or automation wrapper that blocks the call. The old code explicitly tolerated a nullish handle. With this change, reading `.refresh` on null throws a TypeError synchronously, so calling the patched `setTimeout` crashes instead of returning. The fix uses optional chaining (`handleOrId?.refresh`) so a nullish handle is treated as non-refreshable.

findings.description: When the native setTimeout/setInterval/setImmediate/requestAnimationFrame returns a non-number that is also null or undefined (some polyfills or browsers do this, and the old code explicitly guarded for it), the new else branch evaluates `handleOrId.refresh`. That throws a TypeError inside scheduleTask, so scheduling crashes where it previously worked and returned the task.

The code now uses truthiness checks (`if (handleId)`) instead of `typeof === 'number'`. A numeric handle of 0 is treated as no handle, so it is never stored in tasksByHandleId and is not cleaned up. clearTimeout(0) then cannot find the task, and the function returns the task object instead of 0.

It says a nullish return ("undefined or null (polyfills or odd environments)") now throws a TypeError while scheduling. It proposes the same fix, `handleOrId?.refresh`.

When it is not a number, it executes `data.isRefreshable = isFunction(handleOrId.refresh)`. findings.description: In scheduleTask, any non-number result from the native setter is assumed to be an object, so `handleOrId.refresh` is read unconditionally. The old code explicitly allowed setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate and requestAnimationFrame to return undefined or null (polyfills or odd environments). With such a return value this now throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'refresh')` while scheduling, which is a regression. The lookup should be guarded, for example with `handleOrId?.refresh`.

justification: The known bug: selector parts with parentheses can now contain newlines, and `/([^:]*)(:*)(.*)/` drops everything after the first newline. Finding [0] is about shared mutable instance state (`_shouldScopeIndicator`/`_safeSelector`) across recursive calls. It does not mention newlines or the `(.*)` regex truncation, so it is a different defect.
ground_truth: In `ShadowCss._scopeSelector`/`_applySelectorScope`, the change replaced the simple `/ ?, ?/` comma split and the combinator separator with regexes that do not split inside parentheses. A selector part like `.foo:is(.a,\n.b)` therefore now reaches `_scopeSelectorPart` as a single string that can contain newlines. That function splits the part with `/([^:]*)(:*)(.*)/`, both in the newly added pseudo-function `:host` branch (`scopedP.match(...)`) and in the non-host branch (`t.match(...)`). Because `.` does not match a newline, everything after the first newline is silently dropped. For example, a component style `.foo:is(.a,\n.b) {}` is emitted as `.foo[contenta]:is(.a,`, with the rest of the selector and the closing parenthesis lost, which breaks the stylesheet. The fix changed the trailing group of both regexes to `([\s\S]*)` so content after newlines is kept.

findings.description: The scoping state (`_safeSelector` and `_shouldScopeIndicator`) is stored as mutable instance fields shared across recursive `_scopeSelector` and `_applySelectorScope` calls. Nested pseudo-function calls (`isParentSelector` false) can change `_shouldScopeIndicator`, which the outer call then reads for its remaining parts. For example, a `:host` inside `:is()`/`:where()` can flip scoping for later sibling parts or comma alternatives. Edge cases such as `:where(:host) .a, .b` or several nested pseudo functions in one selector could be scoped or left unscoped incorrectly. Nesting also depends on `_safeSelector` not being replaced mid-call.

justification: The known bug: newlines inside parenthesized selector parts are lost because `/([^:]*)(:*)(.*)/` uses `.`, which does not match newlines. Finding [0] is about `slice(prefix.length, -1)` assuming the part ends with the closing paren when there is a suffix such as `:is(.foo):hover`. That is a different mechanism, and it says nothing about newlines or the `(.*)` group.

A selector part like `.foo:is(.a,\n.b)` therefore now reaches `_scopeSelectorPart` as a single string that can contain newlines. That function splits the part with `/([^:]*)(:*)(.*)/`, both in the newly added pseudo-function `:host` branch (`scopedP.match(...)`) and in the non-host branch (`t.match(...)`). Because `.` does not match a newline, everything after the first newline is silently dropped. For example, a component style `.foo:is(.a,\n.b) {}` is emitted as `.foo[contenta]:is(.a,`, with the rest of the selector and the closing parenthesis lost, which breaks the stylesheet. findings.description: `_pseudoFunctionAwareScopeSelectorPart` treats any part that starts with `:where(` or `:is(` as if it also ends with the matching `)`. It slices off the last character with `slice(prefix.length, -1)` and then appends `)`. For a part with a suffix after the function, such as `:is(.foo):hover`, `:where(.a).b` or `:where(a):where(b)`, the slice drops a character that is not the closing paren. The inner text is then scoped incorrectly and a stray `)` is appended. For example, `:is(.foo):hover` is rewritten around the inner text `.foo):hove`, which gives broken or incorrect CSS. The concatenated-pseudo case is only papered over in the tests, where an `xit` documents the wrong output.

justification: The only finding concerns missing Bazel load statements in BUILD.bazel. It says nothing about `metadata.dependencies` being left undefined when `injector` is null, or about the template reading `dependencies.length` and throwing as a result. It is a different concern, so it does not match the known bug.
ground_truth: In `getLatestComponentState` (component-tree.ts), the change wraps `metadata.dependencies = getDependenciesForDirective(...)` in `if (injector)`. Previously `dependencies` was always assigned on the directive metadata. Now `getInjectorFromElementNode` returns null whenever `ng.getInjector` is not supported (or returns nothing), and in that case `dependencies` is left `undefined`. The DevTools property view template evaluates `controller().directiveMetadata?.dependencies.length > 0`. The optional chain only guards `directiveMetadata`, not `dependencies`. So when an app's global `ng` lacks `getInjector`, selecting a component throws a TypeError reading `length` of undefined and the property panel breaks. The fix guards the template by first checking that `dependencies` exists before reading its `length`.

findings.description: The new `ts_test_library` and `karma_web_test_suite` targets are appended, but this hunk adds no matching `load(...)` statements, unlike the ng-debug-api BUILD file. If the lib BUILD file does not already load these symbols, Bazel analysis of the package fails and breaks every target in it.

justification: Finding 0 matches the part of the known bug about the effect body. It says the afterRenderEffect "calls init() on every run, so each new explorer view re-registers the 'highlightComponent' message-bus listener... It also re-creates both InjectorTreeVisualizers each time." The ground truth names this same faulty code and mechanism, and the fix calls init() only once. It does not mention the hidden-tab D3 layout errors, but it points at the same effect and would lead a maintainer to it. Finding 1 is about provider sorting, which is unrelated. Finding 2 claims [hidden] is overridden by :host display, so tabs stay visible. That is a different mechanism, essentially the opposite of the known bug, where the element is hidden with display:none.
ground_truth: This change rewrites `InjectorTreeComponent` to render from an `afterRenderEffect` that runs whenever the `componentExplorerView` input changes. The effect calls `init()` and `updateInjectorTreeVisualization(view.forest)` without checking whether the tab is visible. The change also hides the deferred `ng-injector-tree` with `[hidden]` (display:none) and removes the old `ng-injector- tree.hidden` CSS, which had kept the element laid out with `visibility: hidden`. So once the Injector Tree tab has been opened and the user switches to another tab, every new component explorer view re-runs the effect. D3 then tries to lay out, translate and snap SVG trees inside an element with no layout, which throws errors. `init()` also runs on every effect execution, re-registering the `highlightComponent` listener and recreating the visualizers each time. The fix adds a `hidden` input bound to the host's `[hidden]`, returns early from the effect when it is true (read untracked), and calls `init()` only once, when the visualizers do not exist yet.

findings.description: The afterRenderEffect tracks componentExplorerView and diDebugAPIsAvailable. It calls init() on every run, so each new explorer view re-registers the 'highlightComponent' message-bus listener, producing duplicate handlers. It also re-creates both InjectorTreeVisualizers each time, which discards zoom/pan state and may leave selectedNode pointing at stale nodes. The listener setup and visualizer creation should run once, not on every update.

The component defines sortedProviders (sorted by token), but the template still passes the raw providers() input to ng-injector-providers. Providers are therefore no longer sorted alphabetically, which regresses the previous behaviour where they were sorted before being set.

Tabs are now hidden with the [hidden] attribute instead of a CSS class with display:none. The tab components set :host { display: block/flex } in their own styles, which overrides the browser's [hidden] rule. Inactive tabs, such as the Components explorer, may therefore stay visible and render alongside the active tab.

Under `display:none`, later graph updates while the tab is hidden may compute wrong sizes." That is the core failure: D3 lays out trees inside a `display:none` element. findings.description: The afterRenderEffect write callback runs on every `componentExplorerView` change, and it calls `init()` each time. Each call registers another `highlightComponent` message-bus listener, so listeners accumulate and the highlight handler fires multiple times. It also re-runs `setUpEnvironmentInjectorVisualizer` and `setUpElementInjectorVisualizer` on every update, which recreates both D3 visualizers. The template passes `providers()` to `ng-injector-providers`. The sorted `sortedProviders` computed is never used, and the parent now sets the raw unsorted list. Providers are therefore no longer sorted by token, which regresses the previous behavior.

Visibility is now toggled with the `hidden` attribute and the `.hidden` CSS class is removed. The `hidden` attribute only maps to the UA stylesheet's `display:none`. Any component whose `:host` sets `display` (block or flex) overrides it, so inactive tabs may stay visible. The old `.hidden` class was needed for exactly this reason. In addition, the injector tree previously used `visibility:hidden` with `position:absolute` so D3 could still measure layout while hidden. Under `display:none`, later graph updates while the tab is hidden may compute wrong sizes.

`diDebugAPIsAvailable` is now computed from the current view. It is false whenever the view is null or the forest is empty. The 'only available on version 17.0.0 or higher' message therefore shows before the first view arrives, or when the forest is temporarily empty. The `@else` branch also destroys the whole tree DOM in that case. Previously the flag was only ever set to true and never reverted.

justification: Finding 1 matches the known bug. It says that when "the final segment is a property or method on the related model rather than a model field", `get_fields_from_path` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` unguarded, turning "a previously working display into a crash". That is the same faulty code and the same failure mechanism as the known bug. Finding 0 does not match. It describes a different issue: a ForeignKey final field being mishandled in `items_for_result`, not the uncaught `FieldDoesNotExist` for non-field paths.
ground_truth: The change makes `lookup_field()` in `django/contrib/admin/utils.py` call `get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)[-1]` unconditionally whenever a `list_display` name contains `__`, so it can render boolean icons for related BooleanFields. Before this, such names were resolved only by walking attributes with `getattr`, which also works for paths whose last part is not a concrete model field, such as a method, a property or `__str__` on a related model. `get_fields_from_path` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` for those paths, and the exception is not caught. Because `lookup_field` is shared by the changelist and readonly-field rendering, entries traversing relations, including second-degree ones (e.g. `book__author__get_full_name` or `parent__parent__some_property`), now crash with an exception where they previously displayed fine. The fix removes this lookup from `lookup_field`. It instead resolves the final field only in `items_for_result` when `f` is None, wrapped in `try/except FieldDoesNotExist`.

findings.description: `lookup_field` now returns the final related field `f` for `a__b` lookups, but callers such as `items_for_result` assume `f` belongs to the row object. For a ForeignKey final field (`remote_field` is a `ManyToOneRel`), `items_for_result` calls `getattr(result, f.name)` on the wrong model. That raises `AttributeError` or shows the wrong value, for example for `list_display = ['parent__parent']`. Previously `f` was always `None` on this path, so the value was rendered correctly.

`get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)` is called whenever the attribute traversal succeeds and the name contains `__`. If the final segment is a property or method on the related model rather than a model field, the traversal succeeds but `get_fields_from_path` raises `FieldDoesNotExist` or `NotRelationField`. The unguarded exception turns a previously working display into a crash, for example `list_display` with `'parent__some_property'` or custom attribute paths.

findings.description: `get_fields_from_path(opts.model, name)[-1]` is called unconditionally for any `__` name that resolves through the `getattr` traversal. The traversal also resolves properties, methods and reverse accessors on the related object, for example `parent__some_property`. `get_fields_from_path` only handles real model fields, so for those names it raises `FieldDoesNotExist` or `NotRelationField`. The exception is raised inside the `except` handler, so it is not caught and the changelist crashes with a 500. Previously these names rendered fine. A related ForeignKey or relation as the final field also now gets a non-None `f`, which changes how `items_for_result` renders the value. The call is also indented inside the `for part` loop, so it runs on every iteration instead of once after the loop.

justification: Finding 0 concerns ForeignKey fields: it says `ModelChoiceField.to_python` runs a query per term and applies custom default manager filtering. The known bug is different. It is about `TypedChoiceField.to_python` returning raw strings for choice fields, which causes a ValueError and HTTP 500, and about `BooleanField.to_python` being too lenient. Finding 0 describes neither mechanism, so it does not match.
ground_truth: The change rewrote `ModelAdmin.get_search_results` so that, for non-text `__exact` search fields, each search term is validated with `validate_field.formfield().to_python(bit)`. Lookups whose term raises `ValidationError` are skipped; all others are passed to the ORM with the converted value. This validation does not reject invalid terms for two kinds of fields. First, fields with `choices` produce a `TypedChoiceField`, whose `to_python()` returns the raw string unchanged. So searching "john" against an `IntegerField(choices=...)` with `field__exact` sends "john" to the ORM, which raises `ValueError` and makes the changelist return HTTP 500. Second, `forms.BooleanField.to_python()` maps almost any non-false string to True, so an arbitrary term like "xyz" against `bool__exact` matches every row where the field is True instead of matching nothing. The fix uses `formfield.clean()` for Typed(Multiple)ChoiceField so values are coerced and validated, and uses strict boolean and null-boolean parsers that raise `ValidationError` for unrecognized strings.

findings.description: For `fk__exact` search fields, `prev_field` is the ForeignKey, so `validate_field.formfield().to_python(bit)` goes through `ModelChoiceField.to_python`. That runs a database query (`queryset.get(...)`) for every search term and every such field. It also routes the lookup through the related model's default manager and `to_field_name`, so objects hidden by a custom default manager raise ValidationError and are silently skipped. The old Cast-based approach did no per-term queries and applied no manager filtering. Search results can therefore differ, and each search issues extra queries.

It also relies on formfield().to_python, but the failure mechanism is different, and it mentions neither choices fields nor booleans.

findings.description: A search field like `fk__exact` makes `prev_field` the ForeignKey. Its `formfield()` is a `ModelChoiceField`, and `to_python` on it runs a database query for every search term. It also applies `limit_choices_to` and the field's queryset, so valid values outside that queryset are silently skipped. It returns a model instance instead of the raw value. The old Cast approach did none of this. This adds N queries per search and can change results for relation exact lookups. For these fields, validation should use the model field's own `to_python`/`get_prep_value`, or the related target field, rather than the form field.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same faulty code and mechanism. It quotes `wrap()` returning "an empty list for blank or whitespace-only lines such as '\n', so blank lines and paragraph breaks are dropped". It also notes that a trailing newline is stripped. Both behaviors match the known bug.
ground_truth:
The rewritten `django.utils.text.wrap()` loops over `text.splitlines(True)`, passes each line to `textwrap.TextWrapper.wrap()`, and joins the pieces with "
". `TextWrapper.wrap()` returns an empty list for an empty or whitespace-only line, so those lines vanish from the output. With the default `replace_whitespace=True`, the trailing newline kept by `splitlines(True)` becomes a space and is dropped, so a trailing newline in the input is lost too. For example, `wordwrap("first

second
", 80)` returns "first
second" instead of "first

second
", which merges paragraphs in templates. The fix sets `replace_whitespace=False` and splits with `splitlines()` (no kept ends). It appends the original line whenever the wrapper returns nothing, and appends a final empty element when the text ends with "
".

findings.description:
The rewrite changes how newlines are handled. Each line from `splitlines(True)` goes through `TextWrapper.wrap()`, and the results are joined with '
'. `wrap()` returns an empty list for blank or whitespace-only lines such as '
', so blank lines and paragraph breaks are dropped. For example, 'a

b' becomes 'a
b'. A trailing newline is also stripped, so 'abc
' becomes 'abc'. The old implementation preserved both, so `wordwrap` output for multi-paragraph text regresses. In addition, `TextWrapper` collapses tabs and other whitespace by default (`replace_whitespace=True`), and this was not done before.

The rewritten `django.utils.text.wrap()` loops over `text.splitlines(True)`, passes each line to `textwrap.TextWrapper.wrap()`, and joins the pieces with "
". `TextWrapper.wrap()` returns an empty list for an empty or whitespace-only line, so those lines vanish from the output. With the default `replace_whitespace=True`, the trailing newline kept by `splitlines(True)` becomes a space and is dropped, so a trailing newline in the input is lost too. For example, `wordwrap("first

second
", 80)` returns "first
second" instead of "first

second
", which merges paragraphs in templates. The fix sets `replace_whitespace=False` and splits with `splitlines()` (no kept ends). It appends the original line whenever the wrapper returns nothing, and appends a final empty element when the text ends with "
".

findings.description:
The rewrite changes behavior for newlines and whitespace. `wrapper.wrap(line)` returns `[]` for empty or whitespace-only lines, so blank lines, including paragraph separators like `

`, but `TextWrapper` replaces it with a space and then drops it, so a trailing newline in the input is lost. Whitespace-only lines and leading or trailing whitespace are also removed. Existing `wordwrap` behavior, which preserved these, regresses; for example `wrap('a

b', 10)` now returns `'a
b'`.

justification: Finding 0 matches the known bug. It points at the same check, `"." in str(filter_expression.var)`, and gives the same mechanism: the check "also matches quoted string literals and translated constants, not just variable lookups." It cites the same kind of example (`{{ "a..b"|upper }}`) and the same consequence, a spurious warning that would become an error later. It also proposes the same fix of restricting the check to real variable lookups.
ground_truth: The new deprecation check in `Parser.parse()` for variable nodes tests `".." in str(filter_expression.var)`. For constant expressions, `filter_expression.var` is the resolved literal value (a string or translated string), not a `Variable` lookup. So a template containing a literal with two consecutive dots, such as `{{ "a..b" }}` or `{{ 'a..b'|upper }}`, wrongly emits a `RemovedInDjango70Warning` about double-dot lookups. That warning becomes an exception when warnings are treated as errors. The check would also reject valid templates once it is elevated to an error as planned. The fix applies the check only when the expression is a variable lookup: `filter_expression.is_var and ".." in filter_expression.var.var`.

findings.description: The check `".." in str(filter_expression.var)` also matches quoted string literals and translated constants, not just variable lookups. Once the deprecation ends, the commented-out code would raise TemplateSyntaxError for these valid templates. The check should only apply to real variable lookups, not literals.

justification: Finding 0 is about single-column FKs, NULL handling and IN-list chunking now going through TupleIn. That is a different concern from the known bug. Finding 1 does point at the same line, the hardcoded `queryset.model._meta.db_table` alias in ColPairs. But its mechanism differs: it says the alias may not exist in the query "if the supplied prefetch queryset already carries a custom alias or an earlier join/combinator". The known bug is a mismatch between the alias's model and the fields' model. `foreign_related_fields` belong to the FK target (e.g. Place), while the alias comes from a custom prefetch queryset's model (e.g. a Restaurant MTI child). The parent's columns are then referenced on the child table. Finding 1 never notes that `related_fields` belong to a different model than `queryset.model`, and never mentions subclass or MTI querysets. It therefore describes a different failure scenario.
ground_truth: `ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.get_prefetch_querysets()` now filters with `TupleIn(ColPairs(queryset.model._meta.db_table, related_fields, related_fields, self.field), ...)`, where `related_fields = self.field.foreign_related_fields`. Those are fields of the FK's target model, but the table alias comes from the prefetch queryset's model. With a custom prefetch queryset on a multi-table- inheritance subclass of the target, the two do not match. Example: a FK to `Place` prefetched with `Prefetch("place", queryset=Restaurant.objects.all())`. The generated SQL references the parent's column (e.g. `id`) on the child's table, which has no such column, so `prefetch_related` crashes with a database error. The old `field__in` kwarg filter resolved the field names through the ORM and did not have this problem. The fix resolves each field by name against the prefetch queryset (`queryset.query.resolve_ref(field.name).target`), so the columns match the queryset's model.

findings.description: The old single-column case used a plain `field__in` lookup. That lookup deduplicated values, skipped NULLs, and chunked IN lists for backends with `max_in_list_size` (Oracle). It now always builds a `TupleIn` over a one-element `ColPairs`, even for ordinary single-column FKs, and passes all instance keys as one-element tuples. This pushes every simple forward-FK prefetch through the tuple lookup path. On backends without tuple-lookup support, the result is a large OR-of-ANDs expression that can exceed expression-depth or in-list limits. Instances whose FK is NULL now put `(None,)` into the list, which the old code would not do cleanly. Single-field prefetches can therefore regress in SQL shape and robustness.

`ColPairs` is built with `queryset.model._meta.db_table` as the alias, not the query's actual base alias. If the supplied prefetch queryset already carries a custom alias or an earlier join/combinator, the column references may point at a table alias that does not exist in the query. That would produce wrong SQL or an error.

justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says that passing `writer="html"` only works on docutils 0.22+, that older versions require a Writer instance, and that the call "fails with an AttributeError", which would break parse_rst and the admindocs views. This matches the known bug's mechanism and symptom.
ground_truth: In `django/contrib/admindocs/utils.py`, `parse_rst()` was changed to call `docutils.core.publish_parts(..., writer="html", ...)` instead of `writer_name="html"`, to silence a deprecation warning in docutils 0.22+. Passing a string writer name through the `writer` parameter only works in docutils 0.22+. In docutils 0.19–0.21, `writer` must be a writer instance. With an older docutils installed, every admindocs reStructuredText rendering (docstrings for views, models, template tags, filters) therefore fails, typically with an AttributeError when docutils treats the string "html" as a writer object. The fix creates an instance with `docutils.writers.get_writer_class("html")()` and passes that as `writer`, which works across docutils 0.19 through 0.22.

findings.description: Replacing `writer_name="html"` with `writer="html"` is only safe on docutils 0.22+, where the `writer` argument accepts a name string. On older supported versions, `writer` must be a Writer instance, and `writer_name` is what selects the writer. A string passed as `writer` is kept as-is, so the writer name falls back to the default 'pseudoxml' or the call fails with an AttributeError when the Publisher calls the writer's methods. That would break `parse_rst`, and so the admindocs views, for users on older docutils. The change needs a version check or has to keep `writer_name` for older docutils.

justification: Finding 0 points to the same defect: the new buttons are "created without type=\"button\", so they default to type=\"submit\" inside the admin form", and it suggests setting type="button". The finding does not name the implicit-submission-on-Enter scenario and argues that preventDefault limits the risk. Even so, the faulty code and the root cause (default submit type) are the same, and the suggested fix is exactly the actual fix, so it would have led a maintainer to the bug.
ground_truth: In `SelectFilter.init` in SelectFilter2.js, the change replaced the "Choose all", "Choose selected", "Remove selected" and "Remove all" `<a>` links with `<button>` elements built via `quickElement('button', ...)`. None of them is given a `type` attribute. Inside a form, a button with no type defaults to `type="submit"`. When a user presses Enter in a text input of an admin change form containing a filter_horizontal/filter_vertical widget, the browser's implicit submission activates the first submit button in tree order. If one of these selector buttons comes first, its click handler fires (moving options, with the event default prevented) instead of the form being saved. The fix adds `'type', 'button'` to all four buttons so they no longer act as submit buttons.

findings.description: The new <button> elements are created without type="button", so they default to type="submit" inside the admin form. The click handlers currently call e.preventDefault(), which prevents submission. Any path that bypasses those handlers, such as a handler change or a click that does not reach them, would submit the form. Setting type="button" would be more robust.

justification: Finding [0] identifies the same defect. It says the check uses `self.fields`, which "keeps the '-' prefix on descending fields", while the old code used `fields_orders`. It also states this causes a bogus E012 nonexistent field error for '-name'. Findings [1] and [2] describe different issues: duplicated warnings and the generator bug in [1], and checks running only per database in [2].

The old Model-level check used the field names from `index.fields_orders`, which has that prefix stripped. As a result, a valid index such as `models.Index(fields=["-name"], name="idx")` now fails the system check with "'indexes' refers to the nonexistent field '-name'" (models.E012). The fix passes `field for field, _ in self.fields_orders` instead of `self.fields`.

findings.description: The local-field check uses `self.fields`, which keeps the '-' prefix on descending fields (e.g. `fields=['-name']`). The old code used `fields_orders`, which strips the prefix. Now `_check_local_fields` looks up the field '-name' and reports a bogus 'refers to the nonexistent field' error (models.E012) for valid descending indexes. The fields are also put in a set, so error ordering is nondeterministic.

W037 is computed with `any(self.condition is not None for index in model._meta.indexes)`. justification: Finding 0 identifies the same defect. It says `window.relatedWindows` is undefined in production because the array is module-local, so `.indexOf` throws a TypeError "before `win.close()`" and the popup never closes. The fix went back to the module- local `relatedWindows`, exported it as `window.relatedWindows = relatedWindows`, and removed the test's own initialization.

justification: The known bug is about `returning_fields.remove(field)` dropping db_returning fields that have explicit values, which leaves stale in-memory values even on RETURNING-capable backends. Finding [0] is about the append branch instead: it says "an expression-valued field is appended to `returning_fields` without checking whether it is already there". That is a different code path and a different failure mechanism (duplicate columns rather than removal), so it does not match.
ground_truth: In the insert branch of `Model._save_table`, the change builds `returning_fields = list(meta.db_returning_fields)` and then, for each insert field, calls `returning_fields.remove(field)` (the `elif field.db_returning:` branch) whenever the field's pre_save value is not an expression. Before this change, every `db_returning` field was always fetched back via RETURNING and assigned to the instance. Now a `db_returning` field with an explicitly set value keeps the in-memory Python value instead of the value the database actually stored. This happens even on backends that support RETURNING (PostgreSQL, SQLite, Oracle). For example, an explicitly set primary key or a custom `db_returning=True` field whose stored or converted value (via `from_db_value`, normalization or triggers) differs from the assigned value is left stale on the instance after `save()`/`create()`. The fix only removes such fields from `returning_fields` when the backend cannot return columns from insert, and never removes the auto field when the pk was set.

findings.description: In the insert path, an expression-valued field is appended to `returning_fields` without checking whether it is already there. `meta.db_returning_fields` already contains fields with a `db_default`. If such a field is given an expression (e.g. `Now()`) on insert, it appears twice in `returning_fields`. That gives a duplicated column in the RETURNING clause, and the returned value is assigned twice. On backends without insert RETURNING, the field list is misaligned with the returned values. A membership check (`if field not in returning_fields`) is needed.

justification: Finding 0 states that get_supported_language_variant() "now raises ValueError for over-long codes" while "callers ... only catch LookupError". It uses get_language_from_path/LocaleMiddleware as the example, where an over-500-char prefix with no hyphen causes an "uncaught ValueError and returns a 500". This is the same defect and the same failure mechanism as the known bug.
ground_truth: The security patch added a length check to `get_supported_language_variant()`. When `lang_code` exceeds `LANGUAGE_CODE_MAX_LENGTH` (500) and no generic variant can be cut off (or `strict=True`), it raises `ValueError("'lang_code' exceeds the maximum accepted length")`. This breaks the function's documented contract of raising `LookupError` when nothing is found. Callers like `LocaleMiddleware` and `get_language_from_path()`/`get_language_from_request()` only catch `LookupError`, and with the default strict=False a long code without a usable "-" still reaches the `ValueError` branch. So a request whose URL language prefix or language cookie is longer than 500 characters crashes with an unhandled ValueError (HTTP 500) instead of falling back to another language. Fixed by raising `LookupError(lang_code)` instead of ValueError.

A request such as `/xxxx…(>500 chars)/` handled by LocaleMiddleware or i18n_patterns, with no hyphen in the prefix or with strict=True, now raises an uncaught ValueError and returns a 500 instead of None or a 404. The new exception is a regression for existing callers.

justification: Finding [0] does flag the `field.db_type()` cast, but it describes a different defect. It says the cast breaks on serial types, JSONField, range/hstore and GIS fields, and that the path ignores get_placeholder. It never mentions length/precision parameters such as varchar(50) or numeric(5,2), which cause silent truncation or rounding instead of a 'value too long' error.
ground_truth: The new `SQLInsertCompiler.assemble_as_sql` in the PostgreSQL compiler builds each UNNEST placeholder as `(%s)::<db_type>[]`, where `db_type` comes from `field.db_type(self.connection)`. That type string includes the column's parameters, e.g. `varchar(50)` or `numeric(5, 2)`. In PostgreSQL an explicit cast to a length- limited type silently truncates or rounds values instead of raising an error. So `bulk_create()` of two or more objects whose CharField value exceeds `max_length` silently inserts a truncated string, where the regular VALUES insert would fail with a "value too long" error. The same applies to rounding of decimals. The fix strips the parameters from the type (`db_type.split("(")[0]`), so the cast is to e.g. `varchar[]` and the column's own constraints apply on insert.

findings.description: The UNNEST path builds the cast from `field.db_type()` for every non-array field. That breaks for fields whose `db_type` is not a valid array element type. AutoField/BigAutoField/SmallAutoField return `serial`/`bigserial`, and `(%s)::serial[]` is invalid SQL, so a bulk_create with explicit pk values now raises a ProgrammingError. Other field types also fail: JSONField (the Jsonb adapter can't be sent as an array element), range and hstore fields, and GIS geometry fields with a custom placeholder. This path also ignores `field.get_placeholder()`. Only array fields are excluded, so previously working bulk_create calls can now crash or insert wrong data.

Finding 0 is about `serial` types not being valid cast targets, which is a different failure mechanism. Finding 1 is about the array detection missing sized arrays like `integer[5]`. Neither mentions truncation or rounding from parameterized types.

That type string includes the column's parameters, e.g. `varchar(50)` or `numeric(5, 2)`. findings.description: The UNNEST path builds casts from `field.db_type()` instead of `cast_db_type()`. For AutoField, BigAutoField and SmallAutoField, `db_type` returns `serial`, `bigserial` or `smallserial`. These are not valid cast targets, so `(%s)::serial[]` is a PostgreSQL syntax error. `bulk_create` with two or more objects that set explicit primary keys on an auto field, or an insert that includes such a field, will crash instead of inserting.

The array check uses `endswith("[]")`, which misses ArrayField with a size, whose `db_type` is e.g. `integer[5]`. Such fields are not excluded, so UNNEST flattens the nested array values and the insert fails or inserts wrong data. The check should be `endswith("]")`.

justification: The known bug concerns the namedtuple typename "Attachment" not matching the module attribute name "EmailAttachment", which causes a PicklingError. Finding [0] instead addresses backward compatibility: plain tuples appended directly to `alternatives` would cause an AttributeError in `_create_alternatives`. It never mentions pickling or the typename/variable-name mismatch, so it describes a different issue.
ground_truth: The change adds the module-level `EmailAttachment = namedtuple("Attachment", ["filename", "content", "mimetype"])` in `django/core/mail/message.py`. `EmailMessage.attach()` now stores each attachment as an instance of it. No `Attachment` attribute exists in `django.core.mail.message`; the class is bound to the name `EmailAttachment`. The fix renames the namedtuple type names to match their variable names (`namedtuple("EmailAttachment", ...)`, and likewise `EmailAlternative`).

justification: The known bug is a TypeError in is_valid_ipv6_address when it receives a non-string input (an IPv6Address instance or an int), because len() is called on it. Finding [0] describes a different TypeError: `len(ip_str) > None` when max_length=None is passed to the form field. That is a different trigger and different code path (the form's to_python), not non-string inputs to is_valid_ipv6_address. It does not match.
ground_truth: The change makes `is_valid_ipv6_address()` call the new helper `_ipv6_address_from_str()` instead of `ipaddress.IPv6Address(ip_str)`. The helper begins with `if len(ip_str) > max_length`, and `is_valid_ipv6_address()` still only catches `ValueError`. Before, non-string values that `ipaddress.IPv6Address` accepts, such as an `ipaddress.IPv6Address` instance or an int, were handled. justification: Finding 0 targets the faulty guard in `updateRelatedSelectsOptions`. It notes the guard checks `SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]` rather than the target select, and that "the check is also unrelated to the select being updated." That is the root defect: the code never checks whether `select` is managed by SelectBox, and the fix adds `SelectBox.cache[select.id]`. The finding's main symptom is the inverse case (a missed cache update) rather than the TypeError on plain selects, so this is a borderline match. Still, it points at the same faulty condition and implies the same fix, which would lead a maintainer to the bug.
ground_truth: The change added a block to `updateRelatedSelectsOptions` in RelatedObjectLookups.js that, after appending a new option to another related select, calls `SelectBox.add_to_cache(select.id, option)` and `SelectBox.redisplay(select.id)`. The guard is only `window.SelectBox !== undefined && !SelectBox.cache[currentSelect.id]`; it never checks that `select` itself is managed by SelectBox. Consider a form with several relations to the same model where only some use `filter_horizontal`, so SelectBox.js is loaded. Adding an object via the '+' popup then reaches other plain `<select>` widgets that have no `SelectBox.cache` entry. `add_to_cache` then pushes onto an undefined cache entry and throws a TypeError. That aborts `dismissAddRelatedObjectPopup`, so the popup window never closes. The fix adds the condition `SelectBox.cache[select.id]`, so the cache is updated only for fields SelectBox actually manages.

justification: Finding 0 identifies exactly the mechanism: "%-formatted with min_length before it is passed to ngettext()... That string does not exist in any translation catalog... error always appears in English." It also proposes the fix of interpolating after translation. Finding 1 points out the removed params={'min_length': ...}. The known fix explicitly restores this, so the finding is part of the same defect in the same faulty change and would point a maintainer to that part of the fix. Finding 0 is the primary match.
ground_truth: The new `MinimumLengthValidator.get_error_message()` applies `% self.min_length` to each string literal before passing it to `ngettext`. The msgids that `ngettext` receives are therefore already formatted strings, such as "This password is too short. It must contain at least 8 characters.". These never match the translation catalog entries, which contain the `%d` placeholder. As a result, with a non-English active language (e.g. French), the too-short password error is always shown untranslated in English. The fix calls `ngettext` with the unformatted singular/plural msgids and applies `% self.min_length` to the translated result. It also restores `params={"min_length": ...}` on the raised `ValidationError`.

findings.description: The message is %-formatted with min_length before it is passed to ngettext(), so the msgid becomes e.g. 'This password is too short. It must contain at least 8 characters.' instead of the template with '%(min_length)d'. That string does not exist in any translation catalog, so the lookup fails and the error always appears in English. This regresses translations of the MinimumLengthValidator error for every non-English locale. The interpolation should happen after translation.

The `params={'min_length': ...}` argument was removed from the ValidationError. Code that reads `error.params['min_length']` or relies on the message being lazily interpolated from params now gets None or a KeyError. This is a backward-compatibility regression for existing users.

justification: Finding 3 says "The queries use the default manager ... and ignore the schema editor's database alias `db`. With multiple databases, the rename reads from and writes to the default database instead of the one being migrated." That is the same defect as the known bug: the ContentType and Permission querysets lack .using(db). The other findings describe different issues: sender registration, the substring match, prefix parsing, and the swallowed IntegrityError.
ground_truth: In the new `RenamePermission._rename`, the code reads `db = schema_editor.connection.alias` but never applies it to the lookups. `ContentType.objects.filter(...)` and `Permission.objects.filter(content_type_id__in=...)` therefore run against the default (router-chosen) database rather than the one being migrated. Running `migrate --database=other` on an app with a `RenameModel` reads and renames permissions in the default database, or finds nothing there. Meanwhile the permissions in the database actually being migrated keep their old codenames and names. The fix adds `.using(db)` to both the ContentType and Permission querysets so the operation works on the migration's database connection.

findings.description: pre_migrate.connect is called without sender=self. pre_migrate is emitted once per app config, so rename_permissions runs once per installed app. Each run inserts another RenamePermission after every RenameModel in the same plan, which leaves duplicate operations. The duplicates run repeatedly, and on backward migrations they are redundant. The handler should be connected with sender=self, as the contenttypes equivalent does.

The ContentType filter uses model__icontains=old_model.lower(), a substring match, instead of an exact match. Renaming model 'Foo' also matches content types such as 'foobar' or 'myfoo' in the same app. Permissions of unrelated models are then renamed to the new model's codenames.

The codename prefix is taken with split('_')[0] and every permission is rewritten to '<prefix>_<newmodel>' with name 'Can <prefix> ...'. Custom permissions such as 'can_publish_foo' or 'publish_foo' are corrupted or collide. For example, 'can_publish_foo' becomes 'can_newmodel'. Only the default add/change/delete/view permissions should be renamed.

The queries use the default manager (Permission.objects, and ContentType via apps) and ignore the schema editor's database alias `db`. With multiple databases, the rename reads from and writes to the default database instead of the one being migrated. Only the atomic block uses `using=db`; the save() does not pass using=db.
IntegrityError is swallowed silently, so a conflicting permission leaves the old permission stale with no warning. The new_name comparison also overwrites any customized permission names.

findings.description: The content type lookup uses `model__icontains=old_model.lower()`, a substring match, instead of an exact match. Renaming `User` to `Customer` also selects content types such as `userprofile` or `superuser` in the same app. Their permissions are then renamed to `add_customer` and so on. This corrupts unrelated models' permissions, and the IntegrityError handler only hides some of the collisions. It should be `model=old_model.lower()`.

Every permission on the content type is rewritten as `<first word of codename>_<newmodel>` with a generated name. Custom permissions from `Meta.permissions` (e.g. `can_publish_oldmodel`, which becomes `can_newmodel`) are clobbered. Permission names built from a custom `verbose_name` are overwritten with the CamelCase-derived default. Only the default add/change/delete/view permissions should be renamed.

The query and save use the default router (`Permission.objects` and `permission.save()` without `using=db`), while only the atomic block uses `schema_editor.connection.alias`. When migrating a non-default database, this reads and writes the wrong database, or the update happens outside the intended transaction. The queryset should use `.using(db)` and the save should pass `using=db`.

justification: Finding 0 describes the same defect. It says the MRO walk "does not skip names that a subclass overrides with a non-property", so a parent `@property foo` that a child shadows ends up wrongly listed. It names the same downstream consumers and proposes the same fix of tracking names already seen.
ground_truth: The rewritten `Options._property_names` iterates over `self.model.__mro__` and adds every name whose value in some `klass.__dict__` is a `property`. It does not check whether a class earlier in the MRO already shadows that name with a non-property attribute. Example: an abstract parent model defines `foo` as a `@property` and a child model overrides `foo` with a plain attribute or a field. `foo` is still reported in the child's `_property_names`. Code that relies on this set then treats the name as a property and mishandles it, for example `Model.__init__`/`_prepare_related_fields` kwargs handling and `QuerySet` create/update_or_create validation. The old `inspect.getattr_static` version resolved the attribute as normal lookup would. The fix tracks names already seen in earlier MRO classes and only counts a property if its name was not defined in a more-derived class.

findings.description: The new MRO walk collects every property found in any class in the MRO. It does not skip names that a subclass overrides with a non-property, such as a field, a method or a plain attribute. The old getattr_static approach only looked at the first definition in the MRO. A parent `@property foo` overridden in a child by a non-property is therefore wrongly listed in `_property_names`. Code that relies on this set (Model.__init__ kwargs handling, QuerySet get_or_create/update_or_create param extraction) will then treat the name as a property, which gives wrong results. The fix is to track names already seen in more-derived classes and ignore properties that were shadowed.

findings.description: The new MRO walk collects every property found in any class's __dict__ without tracking names already shadowed by a more-derived class. The old code used getattr_static, which resolved to the first match in the MRO. If a base class defines a property and a subclass overrides that name with a non-property (a model field, a plain attribute, or None), the name is still reported as a property. Because _property_names is used to decide which names clash with field names, and by QuerySet.update_or_create/get_or_create to reject property names, this can wrongly reject valid kwargs or raise errors for overridden attributes. The fix is to keep a 'seen' set of all names from more-derived classes and skip those.

justification: Finding [0] concerns the `self.output_field` access raising FieldError instead of AttributeError when the output field cannot be resolved. The known bug is different: the `self.output_field != resolved.query.output_field` comparison uses Field equality (creation_counter), so an explicitly passed output_field always triggers ExpressionWrapper wrapping. Finding [0] does not identify that equality comparison or the always-wrap behavior, so it does not match.
ground_truth: The new `Subquery.resolve_expression()` is meant to drop the Subquery shim and return the bare resolved `Query`. It is supposed to wrap the query in an `ExpressionWrapper` only when the user passed an `output_field` that differs from the query's own. It tests this with `self.output_field != resolved.query.output_field`, but `Field.__eq__` compares fields by `creation_counter` and model, not by kind. So a separately instantiated field such as `IntegerField()` never equals the query's model field. As a result, any `Subquery(..., output_field=X())` is always wrapped in an `ExpressionWrapper`, even when `X` is the same field type as the selected column. Lookups that introspect the right-hand side as a `Query` then no longer recognize it, defeating the purpose of the change. One example is the tuple lookups' `isinstance(self.rhs, Query)` check, which is supposed to raise `NotSupportedError` for composite-pk comparisons against subqueries. The fix compares field types (`type(self.output_field) is not type(resolved.query.output_field)`) instead of using field equality.

findings.description: Subquery.resolve_expression only catches AttributeError around `self.output_field`. When the wrapped query has no explicit single select column (e.g. `Subquery(Model.objects.all())` before default columns are added) and no explicit output_field, `Query.output_field` returns None. The cached `output_field` property then raises FieldError ("Cannot resolve expression type, unknown output_field"), not AttributeError. The exception escapes from resolve_expression, so such Subquery expressions now crash at resolution time. Previously the output field was resolved lazily and the expression worked when it was never needed.
